Stochomys longicaudatus, the target rat, is a relatively little-known murid rodent inhabiting the dense undergrowth of Central African forests. Basal metabolic rate measurements obtained from respirometry trials on a small number of individuals under controlled laboratory conditions at a body temperature of 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C] revealed a maximum oxygen consumption of 97.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 97.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour]. This value aligns reasonably well with predictions based on body mass for a murid rodent of this size, though the sample size remains limited. Reproductive output in this species has been documented in captive colonies, where females produce litters ranging from one to four pups [N_R_i = litters ranging from one to four pups] during a single reproductive event. Given the species' relatively low annual reproductive frequency, these modest litter sizes suggest a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality and survival over sheer numerical output.

Reproductive frequency in the target rat has been documented under stable captive conditions maintained at an ambient temperature of 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C]. Females typically produce approximately six litters per year [F_R_i = approximately six litters per year], a rate that is moderate among murid rodents but reflects an intermittent, rather than continuous, breeding pattern. This reproductive schedule, combined with the observed litter sizes, results in a modest annual reproductive output that is consistent with the species' K-selected life-history profile. Birth mass in this species is quite low, with neonates weighing approximately 2.6 grams [Wwb = approximately 2.6 grams] at parturition. This minimal birth mass is typical of altricial murids that undergo a substantial period of intense maternal investment following birth, highlighting the vulnerability of the newborn pups during their initial days of life.

The developmental trajectory of juvenile target rats is characterized by relatively short intervals of maternal dependency. Under captive conditions held at the standard temperature of 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C], the weaning period is completed by 21 days after birth [tx = 21 days after birth]. This relatively early nutritional independence allows the female to redirect her energetic resources toward subsequent reproductive cycles. In parallel, the gestation period itself occupies a span of 21 days [tg = 21 days] when measured under the same thermal conditions. This gestation length is standard for a rodent of this body size and represents a relatively brief interval of embryonic development, a pattern common among altricial murids that produce highly undeveloped neonates requiring extensive post-natal care.

Puberty in Stochomys longicaudatus is reached after a post-natal developmental period of 70 days [tp = 70 days], a duration measured at the species' standard ambient temperature of 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C]. This age at sexual maturation is relatively extended compared to many smaller murid rodents, likely reflecting the energetic demands of attaining the species' relatively large adult body size before the onset of reproductive activity. The ultimate wet weight recorded for adult individuals in this species is approximately 90 grams [Wwi = approximately 90 grams]. This adult body mass places the target rat among the larger-bodied members of its murid community, and this substantial body size is thought to be an adaptation related to its semi-terrestrial, thicket-dwelling lifestyle, where larger body mass may confer advantages in thermoregulation and resource competition.

The weaning mass of juvenile target rats, recorded at the point of nutritional independence, averages 17.5 grams [Wwx = 17.5 grams]. This represents a substantial increase from the birth mass of 2.6 grams [Wwb = 2.6 grams], reflecting a period of rapid growth fueled entirely by maternal milk. The maximum lifespan documented for this species under captive conditions, measured at 34.1 °C [T = 34.1 °C], is approximately 7.3 years [am = approximately 7.3 years]. This longevity is notably high for a murid rodent of 90 grams [Wwi = 90 grams] adult body mass, suggesting a comparatively slow pace of life and low extrinsic mortality in its natural forest habitat. The combination of relatively late maturation, modest reproductive output, and extended lifespan is characteristic of a species occupying a stable, predictable environment where adult survival is prioritized over high fecundity.
